criterion_notes.c1: Yes. The paper focuses on piped drinking water supply and sewage collection and treatment coverage and universalization in Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Yes under both readings. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines legal, institutional, and regulatory reforms in Brazil's water and sanitation sector (Law 11.445/2007 and Law 14.026/2020). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the statutory provisions discussed—utility ownership and contracting rules (prohibiting unbid municipal-state 'program contracts' and mandating competitive concession bidding), contractual universalization targets (99% water and 90% sanitation by 2033), financial-capacity screening of State-owned utilities, federal spending-power conditionality for regionalization and regulatory compliance, and ANA's national tariff and service regulation guidelines—constitute utility ownership, contracting, and regulatory structures directly governing service access. However, these mechanisms are only described doctrinally and prospectively rather than evaluated empirically.
criterion_notes.c3: No. This is a descriptive legal and policy overview / critical commentary written in early 2021 shortly after the July 2020 enactment of Law 14.026/2020. It has no empirical research design, no methodology, no primary data collection, and no systematic empirical synthesis; secondary descriptive statistics (e.g., SNIS 2018/2019 coverage tables, Giambiagi 2021 sector investment shares, Juliatto 2020 agency counts) are cited solely as historical/sector background prior to the 2020 reform, followed by prospective author opinion on future challenges. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Although the paper cites pre-reform aggregate regional water and sanitation coverage figures from SNIS (2018/2019) as background context, it reports no empirical access outcome resulting from the 2020 legal reform, offering only prospective commentary on whether the 2033 universalization goals are likely to be achieved.
criterion_notes.c5: No. Because the article is a non-empirical statutory and policy overview rather than an empirical study, there is no identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or measured exposure-outcome estimate.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. The full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: According to the National Water and Sanitation Information System (SNIS) (2018), 34 million people (16.4% of the population), roughly the population of Canada, still do not have access to drinking water.
This paper examines the state of the water and sanitation services in Brazil before 2020 as well as the potential effects of the recently approved reform.
This paper describes the current state of the WSS in Brazil, the new provisions brought about by the reform approved by the Parliament and the potential impact of the reform.

In summary, the legal changes brought about by the reform can be structured on four pillars that consolidate the main advances in the new legal framework. They are: improvements in the regulatory framework; regionalization of the provision of services; standardization of services provision contracts; and removal of barriers to entry to the private sector.
Therefore, the authors of this paper believe that coverage rates will increase at larger rates, but it is unlikely that the goals stated by the law will be reached.

raw_response.exposure: Law 14.026/2020 (2020 statutory and regulatory reform of the water and sanitation services sector in Brazil)
raw_response.outcome: not reported (prospective discussion of potential future universalization/coverage effects; pre-reform SNIS coverage rates cited only as background)
raw_response.population_and_sample: not reported (national sector-level legal and policy overview of Brazil's water and sanitation sector; no empirical sample)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the article addresses Brazilian water and sanitation service coverage (c1) and examines legal and regulatory rules governing utility ownership, competitive concession bidding, regionalization, and national regulatory guidelines under Law 14.026/2020 (satisfying c2 under both plain and narrow readings), it is a non-empirical legal and policy overview written shortly after the July 2020 enactment of the law. It presents statutory exposition, secondary background sector statistics (pre-reform SNIS tables), and prospective author commentary on future implementation challenges, with no empirical study design, primary data, or empirical evaluation of access outcomes (c3=no, c4=no, c5=no).
